I Spent 20 Years Moving Work Offshore. Now We're Moving Work Off-Human...

For most of my career, when organizations wanted to improve efficiency, reduce costs, or create capacity, the answer was usually some version of the same thing:
~ Move the work.
~ Move it between departments.
~ Move it into shared services.
~ Move it offshore.
~ Move it to lower-cost labor markets.

I spent more than two decades helping organizations do exactly that. Today, I'm seeing something fundamentally different.

We're no longer asking:  "Where should the work go?"
We're asking:  "Should a person be doing the work at all?"

And I think that's especially important in Financial Services and Insurance. One of the industry's biggest challenges has never been average demand. It's surviving the peaks.

- Open enrollment.
- Tax season.
- Back-to-school benefit changes.
- Year-end processing.
- January 1 surges.
- Market volatility.

The peaks can be dramatically higher than the valleys. For decades, we tried to solve that problem with people.

* More hiring.
* More training.
* More overtime.
* More offshore capacity.

The problem never really went away. Because humans aren't elastic; AI is.

For the first time, organizations have access to labor that can expand and contract with demand without recruiting, onboarding, training, scheduling, or backfilling.   That changes the equation.

The conversation is shifting from: "How many people do we need?" to "How much human labor do we actually need?"

That's a subtle difference. But I think it's one of the biggest operating model shifts I've seen in my career. Organizations are still budgeting for headcount. Increasingly, they may need to budget for labor. And labor won't always be human.

Share your experience: What's caused more operational pain in your organization: being understaffed when demand spikes, or being overstaffed when demand returns to normal?

Last week, a new creator equity deal between CatGPT and Smooth Media happened, and the co-founder Jenny Rothenberg said one of the smartest things about creator equity deals I have heard until now.

Cat Goetze (CatGPT) built 1.4M+ followers teaching AI. Smooth Media is the business and talent management company that manages her.

The deal: Cat took an equity stake in Smooth Media and joined as a strategic advisor.

Here is how Jenny framed it:
"Creator equity deals have gone more for distribution and brand than for brain and perspective, and they are working with Cat far more for the latter."

They didn't give equity to borrow her audience. They did it to get her mind.

Most creator equity deals get built the opposite way.

Cash is tight, the product needs attention, and the founder thinks giving equity is a cheap way to buy posts. So they write a contract with a post quota attached to the equity.

On paper it feels like a clever discount on marketing.

In reality, you turned an ownership stake into a sponsorship with extra steps. You set both the floor and the ceiling in the contract. You wanted an owner, but you hired a contractor who clocks out the second the last post goes live.

An owner does not count deliverables against a contract. True equity alignment makes someone act like an owner, finding ways to go above and beyond to move the business. 

Depending on what that creator uniquely brings, that could mean sharpening product positioning, opening doors to key retail buyers, making investor introductions, or helping land critical hires.

None of that fits on a deliverables sheet.

If you are structuring a creator equity deal, bring them in like a true advisor or operating partner. Focus on real business needs (product input, distribution partners, hiring, domain expertise) with real long-term vesting tied to commitment.

When an aligned creator has skin in the game, the posting happens naturally anyway, and it is far more authentic.

Smooth Media understands this. They did not bring on someone to make a couple of posts and clock out. They brought on a true partner for the long term.

A lot of startups and creators can learn from how this was done. And I broke it down in full in this week's newsletter. Comment below, and I will send it to you.

Case Study: Enterprise AI Integration & Governance in Corporate Legal Functions
Executive Summary
Corporate legal departments are at a turning point: balancing rising workload pressures and regulatory complexity against tightening resources. This case study shows how legal functions evolve from reactive cost centers into strategic value‑drivers by deploying a hybrid human/AI agent workforce anchored in robust governance.
Context & Drivers of Transformation:
Technological Disruption: Specialized domain LLMs, agentic workflows, and DIY legal tech solutions.
Regulatory Complexity: Rapidly shifting global rules on AI, privacy, and compliance.
Resource Constraints: Rising transaction volumes with flat hiring budgets.
Strategic Alignment: Executive expectations for legal to drive efficiency and outcomes.
Problem Statement
Legal teams face three operational bottlenecks:
Low ROI on Human Capital: Senior counsel bogged down in routine reviews and discovery.
Compliance Risk: Manual tracking of regulatory changes creates enforcement gaps.
Pace vs. Risk Friction: Business demands speed; legal slows approvals to mitigate liability.
Strategic Framework: Modern Legal Operating Model
1. Hybrid Human/AI Agent Architecture
Routine triage, redlining, and regulatory checks offloaded to AI agents.
HITL oversight for negotiation, risk assessment, and final approvals.
Impact: Faster triage, freeing counsel for strategic advisory.
2. Enterprise AI Governance & Control
Continuous monitoring of regulatory updates into RAG repositories.
Immutable audit trails with statutory citations.
Guardrails defining autonomous vs. human‑signoff tasks.
3. Cross‑Functional Synergy
Chief Data & AI Strategist partners with General Counsel.
Metrics shift from activity‑based (contracts processed) to value‑based (deal velocity, compliance coverage, cost avoidance).
Key Takeaways & Strategic Lessons:
AI Deployment = Operating Model Shift: Not a software upgrade, but a redesign of workflow hierarchies.
Governance Enables Velocity: Guardrails accelerate execution by reducing risk aversion.
Replicable Blueprint: Legal’s hybrid model scales to Risk, Audit, and Regulatory Affairs.

I find it fascinating that recruitment agencies seem to think that burdening prospective customers with lengthy AI generated FOIRs is a sensible way to attract new business. I've seen a spate of requests being sent to schools and trusts that ask for lots of detail about existing suppliers and contracts. I can't believe that these FOIRs will generate useful data that allows a competitive advantage over their competitors, all it achieves is annoying their prospective clients and wasting their limited time.

If any are reading this, rather than use AI to generate an FOIR, how about using this as a prompt:

"Act as an expert B2B copywriter specializing in the UK education sector. Write a high-converting cold email template aimed at UK Headteachers and School Business Managers (SBMs).
Goal: Position our recruitment agency as a time-saving, cost-reducing partner. 
Key Selling Points to Include:
- Rapid response for unexpected staff shortages (same-day cover)
- Measurable workload reduction (handling DBS/safeguarding admin, pre-vetting)
- Budget-friendly rates and transparent pricing compared to standard agencies
- Streamlined, zero-hassle hiring process
Tone & Style: Respectful of their time, empathetic to school pressure, professional, and ultra-concise (under 150 words). Include a low-friction Call to Action (CTA) and 2–3 subject line variations."

You can use that for no charge as long as promise never to send a FOIR to a school or trust trying to generate new business.

A manufacturing executive at Ford sat across from a recently retired engineer, sliding a consulting contract across the table to ask them to come back.

The automaker had attempted to replace experienced engineering headcount with modern AI tools. The outcome was an executive admission that AI could not replicate decades of unwritten, hard-won judgment required to build quality vehicles.

At the same time, tests on HackerRank's open-sourced applicant tracking system showed the exact same resume receiving wildly divergent scores from one run to the next.

If you are designing operational workflows or scaling automated systems, here is a 4-step framework to audit your automation pipeline before it creates structural damage:

1. Map unwritten institutional judgment before cutting headcount
AI models excel at digesting documented data, but fail when critical decisions rely on tacit operational memory. Follow Ford's hard lesson: audit where quality control depends on human nuance and design AI to augment those specialists rather than displace them.

2. Run deterministic variance audits on algorithmic scoring
Before deploying evaluative AI in hiring, underwriting, or screening, feed identical test inputs multiple times. If an applicant scorer swings dramatically on identical data—as HackerRank's tool demonstrated—your model is hallucinating evaluation metrics and poisoning your pipeline.

3. Protect the physical bottlenecks powering your software
Software scale is gated by hardware reality. Notice where smart capital is moving: Omen AI raised $31 million specifically to monitor bacterial outbreaks and biofouling in high-density data center liquid cooling systems. Rocket Lab deployed $8 billion to acquire Iridium Communications for established orbital infrastructure. If your digital stack ignores physical reliability, cooling, or bandwidth bottlenecks, your automation cannot scale.

4. Orchestrate specialized agents rather than relying on monolithic models
Deploy open-source multiplexers like Herdr to run and monitor multiple discrete agents simultaneously directly in the developer terminal. Narrow, specialized models—like Zhipu AI's open-weight GLM-5.2 matching top benchmarks in cybersecurity bug-hunting—consistently outperform bloated single models on mission-critical execution.

Where in your workflow is automation currently outpacing your quality control?

Governor Newsom signed California's newest AI law standing inside SAG-AFTRA's headquarters, flanked by the actors' union whose members have spent two years pushing back on AI replacing them without anyone having to say so. The venue was the message.
SB 1050, signed September 16, requires any video or audio ad running in California after January 1, 2027 to disclose when it uses a "synthetic performer" — an AI-generated face, voice, or figure that plays a foreground role: demonstrating the product, delivering the main pitch, or standing in as a testimonial. The statute spells out acceptable disclosure language ("This performance features a synthetic performer" or "No human performer is depicted"), and enforcement runs through California's existing false-advertising framework, which means platforms can be ordered to pull an ad once a court finds it violates the law.

Here's the move for this quarter: pull every ad currently in production or scheduled to run past January 1 — video, audio, streaming, podcast — and flag any that use an AI-generated voice or performer in a lead role. For each one, decide now where the disclosure lives (on-screen text for video, a spoken line for audio) and get creative and legal to agree on wording before it turns into a rush job in December. Then add a synthetic-performer disclosure clause to every ad-production and influencer contract you sign between now and year-end, so the obligation sits with the agency or creator who built the ad, not just your legal team catching it after the fact.

A few other developments worth tracking this week: the EU AI Office opened its first wave of compliance inspections, with French, German, and Spanish regulators requesting technical documentation and bias-testing records for high-risk AI used in hiring, lending, and healthcare. Newsom also issued a separate executive order convening a working group to recommend AI safety measures — including a possible "kill switch" mandate for frontier models — due back in two months. California's SB 1119 (Adam's Law) tightened companion-chatbot rules for minors, adding independent-auditor review of risk assessments. And the UK's consultation on regulating workplace AI monitoring tools closes September 30.
That ad-review exercise is the kind of thing I'd hand a client in week one — narrow enough to finish by Friday, and it usually surfaces two or three other AI-vendor gaps along the way.

Happy to walk through it if you're staring down a Q4 campaign calendar.

HERE’S SOMETHING I’VE LEARNED AFTER YEARS IN THE WORKFORCE:

You can learn a LOT about a person by watching what they do when nobody is paying them.

When someone is out of work and instead of sitting around waiting, they start a business, build a website, create content, network, learn new skills, help other people, or create something from nothing…

PAY ATTENTION.

That person is showing you initiative.

I’ve been working for a long time, and I’ve done a LOT — full-cycle recruiting, talent acquisition, sourcing, HR, business development, consulting, marketing, websites, content creation, nonprofit leadership, project coordination, AI, music, commercial truck driving and more.

I’m not saying that to toot my own horn.

I’m saying don’t mistake unemployment for incompetence.

People lose jobs because of layoffs, restructuring, budgets, contracts ending and circumstances completely outside their control.

And while they’re looking for their next opportunity, some people sit still.

Others BUILD.

That’s the person I want you to notice.

Because perfect candidates don’t exist.

Creative people do.
Problem-solvers do.
People with initiative do.
People who GET THE JOB DONE do.

So I’m going to keep creating until my next full-time opportunity comes.

Because being unemployed doesn’t mean I’m not working.

I’m working on ME. 🔥

Recruiters and hiring managers: look beyond the employment gap.

Look at what someone has built, led, created and accomplished.

Sometimes the person you’re overlooking is exactly the person you need.

We’re all in this together. 🤝🏽

May this be the week you get your interview.
May this be the week you get your offer.
May this be the week somebody finally sees your value. ❤️‍🔥

And we're already seeing examples of what that future looks like.

A recent article from the Association of Corporate Counsel highlighted how Palo Alto Networks' legal department used Google Gemini to build a tool that allows business users to input key variables, such as counterparty name, contract date, termination date, and reason for termination.
Using pre-approved templates and playbooks, the tool generates a first draft.

The result? Turnaround time for routine documents dropped from 3–5 business days to 1 day.
The legal team also estimated saving 20–40 hours per month.
This is where I think the conversation around AI and the legal profession needs to evolve.

The question is no longer simply:
Can AI draft a contract?

The more important questions are:
• Which agreements can be safely automated?
• How do we establish appropriate guardrails and escalation criteria?
• How does the role of legal professionals evolve as routine drafting becomes more efficient?
• How do we shift our time toward higher-value work that requires legal judgment, negotiation, and strategic business partnership?

In my experience supporting business teams, legal's value involves understanding commercial objectives, identifying risk, negotiating practical solutions, and helping the business move forward.
AI has the potential to change how we deliver that value.

For those working in-house or hiring for legal teams: How do you see AI changing the skills and responsibilities that will matter most for corporate counsel over the next 3–5 years?
I'd be interested in hearing different perspectives.

Another interesting AI opportunity - and this one is for senior enterprise sales, marketing and RevOps professionals.

Mercor is hiring professionals on a remote contract basis at $60–$70/hour to help build evaluation tasks for AI systems working with complex Fortune 500 go-to-market scenarios.

What makes this interesting?

The work isn't about knowing how to code an AI model.

It's about knowing how real enterprise GTM actually works.

The role involves creating scenarios around:

→ $1M+ ACV enterprise sales deals
→ Multi-stakeholder Fortune 500 buying committees
→ Enterprise ABM and demand generation
→ Lifecycle marketing and category positioning
→ Salesforce, Marketo, 6sense, Gong and Outreach
→ MEDDIC, Challenger and Force Management
→ Enterprise procurement, budgets and legal review
→ Building rubrics that distinguish genuine GTM judgment from generic playbook knowledge

The requirement is also very specific:

5+ years of experience selling, marketing or running RevOps within a Fortune 

500 enterprise software vendor, or inside an F500 brand/marketing organization.

This is a useful reminder for experienced professionals:

Your domain expertise can become an AI skill.

You don't necessarily need to leave your existing profession and start from zero in AI.

A senior salesperson may bring enterprise deal judgment.

A marketing leader may bring brand, ABM and demand-generation expertise.

A RevOps professional may bring real-world GTM systems knowledge.

An experienced operator may know what actually happens inside procurement, legal and multi-stakeholder buying processes.

That knowledge is valuable because AI systems need to be evaluated against real-world professional judgment, not just textbook answers.

So if you're a mid-to-senior professional exploring AI opportunities, I would add one more question to your job search:

“What part of my professional judgment could be valuable to an AI system?”

That can lead you to opportunities you may never find by searching only for “AI jobs.”

For job seekers, this is an important shift:

Don't only learn AI. Learn how your existing expertise can work with AI.

A Job Seeker Deserves a Real Opportunity — Not False Hope.

One of the most frustrating parts of today’s job market isn’t rejection. Rejection is understandable. What’s difficult is spending time on an opportunity that may never have been actively moving forward. Candidates receive calls, customize resumes, sign RTRs, share availability, prepare for interviews, and follow up—only to eventually discover that the requirement was already closed, put on hold, duplicated across multiple vendors, or simply disappeared without an update.

Of course, hiring changes. Budgets get frozen, clients pause projects, requirements are cancelled, and other candidates get selected. Every job seeker understands that not every submission will become an interview. The problem isn’t hearing “No.” The problem is being given hope when there is no meaningful opportunity behind it.

Recruiters and vendors are an important part of the hiring ecosystem, especially in the contract market. A little transparency can make that relationship much stronger. If the requirement is active, say so. If the resume was submitted to the client, provide an update when possible. If the position is on hold, communicate it. If the client selected someone else, candidates would rather hear that than continue waiting without clarity.

Candidates also have a responsibility. We should verify the recruiter and company we are dealing with, understand what we are authorizing through an RTR, protect sensitive information, track where our resume is being submitted, and avoid duplicate submissions through multiple vendors.

For me, a healthy recruiting relationship comes down to real opportunities, responsible submissions, clear communication, and mutual respect. Candidates aren’t expecting every recruiter to guarantee an interview or placement. We are simply asking for transparency about what is actually happening.

If the opportunity is active, let’s pursue it. If it closes, tell us. If the client rejects the profile, tell us. If there is genuinely no update, saying “there is no update yet” is completely fine.
Behind every resume is a person managing a career, responsibilities, time, and expectations. Transparency costs very little, but for someone actively searching for their next opportunity, it can mean a lot.

Nscale is going public this week at around a $35B valuation, and the filing shows $103B of contracts already signed. Impressive, until you notice that about 85% of it comes down to just two customers: Microsoft and Anthropic.
And the Anthropic piece isn't even locked in. It depends on Nscale raising the financing to deliver, and Anthropic can walk if they miss targets the filing openly describes as stringent. So a big chunk of that backlog is really a maybe.

The thing is, this isn't unique to Nscale. CoreWeave does two thirds of its revenue with Microsoft. Applied Digital leans the same way on Oracle. Most of the AI infrastructure boom is being paid for by the same small group of buyers, all propping each other up.

It's changed how I look at these companies when I'm hiring for them. A headline backlog doesn't tell you much anymore. What matters is who the customers actually are and how quickly they could leave.
The good engineers have already worked this out. They ask who's really paying the bills before they join, not what the press release says.

I’ve watched resources dwindle rapidly in my past two years at the Herald, a place I was excited to work for. Now, as my own contract comes to an end, roughly a third of the staff has been laid off. My heart goes out to everyone who lost not just a job, but, for many, a place they considered home.
But what’s happening is bigger than that. It’s a devastating blow for the people of Miami, for Florida, and for the country, in ways we have yet to fully comprehend. More often than not, no journalist will be at local commission or school board meetings, and nobody will scrutinize shady politicians or business owners (of which South Florida, of course, has plenty).
I spent almost 15 years as a foreign correspondent, in countries where independent, local journalism had disappeared - often through orchestrated efforts by powerful people who understood that a public that doesn’t know what’s happening is much easier to govern.
I've learned that journalism isn’t a luxury, and that information is power. And without independent journalists, ordinary people lose some of their ability to hold power accountable and make informed decisions about their own lives.
In total, the Herald's owner, the hedge-fund-owned McClatchy, has laid off more than 90 journalists, from Sacramento to Charlotte, from Lexington to Miami. Instead, they're investing in AI, and hiring influencers. Neither can do the work that a newsroom does, but by the time we'll all feel the impact, it'll be too late.
